To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the cooling performance of silicon thermoelectrics is limited by the heat conduction and the heat generation in the substrate, the electric contact resistance, and the thermal resistance of the metal lead, (2) the cooling performance can be improved by increasing the doping concentration and by decreasing the microcooler size, and (3) the peak cooling and the maximum cooling heat flux can be improved by decreasing the microcoolersize.
the peak cooling and maximum surface cooling heat flux can be increased by reducing the metal lead thickness, increasing the doping concentration, and reducing the device size, respectively.
the cooling performance of silicon thermoelectrics is strongly affected by metal leads, electric contact resistance and doping concentrations.
In summary, our research is concerned with

developing an analytical thermal model of a silicon thermoelectric cooler, investigating the effects of the device geometry and the material parameters on the cooling performance of the microcooler, and comparing the modeling results with the experimental and numerical simulation results.
the development of a new class of thermoelectric microdevices, which can be used for thermal management of integrated circuits and other high-performance electronic components.
the analytical modeling of silicon thermally coupled microcoolers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the silicon thermoelectric cooler is a viable on-chip cooling technology for high performance integrated circuits.
the silicon microcooler is an effective and efficient thermoelectric device, and that it can be designed to meet the cooling requirements of advanced integrated circuits.

, in general, the cooling performance of silicon thermoelectrics improves with decreasing silicon doping concentrations, but the cooling performance is not sensitive to the metal lead thickness, and is only slightly affected by electric contact resistance.

the silicon microcooler can achieve a maximum cooling heat flux up to 0.8W/mm ^{2} at a cooling current of 1A.

, with a proper design of silicon microcooler dimensions, doping concentrations, and metal lead, silicon thermoelectric coolers can achieve high cooling potential, comparable to or even better than the state-of-the-art commercial thermoelectric devices.
